method: No source gives any of the fifteen hazards as a function of the date of full automation. Forecasts conditional on timelines exist only for existential catastrophe (a 2022 LessWrong thread of about 40 forecasters, Metaculus question 12840, Greenblatt's risk by lead time, MacAskill and Taylor's 2026 note) and, weakly, for catastrophe and cybercrime under rapid against slow progress (FRI LEAP wave 9). Every factor is therefore a guess. This is the version revised on 20 November 2026 after an independent check (research/ai/ai-leadtime.check.md) and changes to the engine. (1) Reference. The five research files anchor their transition rates on forecasts and defences of 2026 to 2028 and on AGI in about 2027 to 2030; taking 2028.5 and adding about 3.5 years from AGI to full automation gives 2032, five years from the start of 2027. (2) Timing. The turbulent period is the 3.5 years from AGI to automation, reached by a two-year run-up from today's rate; the last 1.5 of the old five years from AGI fall after automation and are carried by afterShare. (3) Shorter leads. Factor = compression (the 3.5 turbulent years in fewer: 3.5 at one year, 1.27 at three) x unpreparedness (1.02 to 1.25) x the share of the squeezed excess that can happen before automation, given the time attackers, strikers, armies and crises need (0.35 to 0.75 at one year, 0.8 to 0.97 at three). The three terms express my judgment of the yearly rate; they are not derivations. (4) Longer leads. Factor = what the extra years of preparation buy, hazard by hazard, from the adaptation speeds in the evidence, down to a floor for risk that comes from the capability itself or from states' choices. The first version also multiplied by a dilution for a longer, slower transition (0.9, 0.78, 0.65, 0.57 at 8, 12, 20 and 30 years); since the engine keeps the turbulent period and the run-up fixed, that removed the excess instead of spreading it, and I have divided it out. Where more lead could make things worse (a longer arms race, China at parity, a late and very fast takeoff, a larger attack surface, a larger debt boom) the high end is above 1. (5) After automation. afterShare is the share of the way from the after rate back to the transition rate just after automation, which the engine fades to zero over the turbulent years. It follows from the old five-year window: 1.5 years of it lie after automation at the reference and more at shorter leads. (6) Existential catastrophe. Its factors come from the conditional forecasts and now act on the odds, as the engine applies them; because the existing 0.2 rests on older statements by people with longer timelines, the factor is 1 at eight years, not five. Low and high values are my 5th and 95th percentiles; the model draws them together with the sceptic-to-concerned spread, so the low end is the view that defenders adapt quickly given time and the high end the view that lead time does not help. Pages were read through a fetch tool that summarises and caps quotations at about 125 characters; the NIST and White House documents were read as PDF text and pages, and the Metaculus figures from the data embedded in the embed pages.

turbulentYears.basis: Changed from 5 after the check. The old window was the five years from AGI; the new one ends at full automation, about 3.5 years after AGI on the views behind the transition figures: 2 to 2.5 in the race ending of AI 2027 (https://ai-2027.com/race), 2.8 between Metaculus's weak and strong AGI medians, about 3 from 20% to 100% of cognitive tasks in Davidson 2023, plus time for robots at scale, which Davidson and Hadshar expect to come more slowly; a decade or more on slow-diffusion views. So the full rate runs from AGI to automation and the last 1.5 of the old five years fall after automation, where afterShare carries them. With five turbulent years the full rate began 1.5 years before AGI, which put a 2032 reader at eight to ten times today's cyber rate throughout 2027. Lo: fast takeoff. Hi: slow diffusion. The true length grows with the lead (openQuestions).

runUpYears.basis: Changed from 3. The engine ramps from today's rate, which is observed at the end of 2026, so the ramp should begin at 2027. For the reference reader the turbulent period begins with AGI at about 2029, two years on. A two-year ramp puts one year-equivalent of excess before AGI against five after it, 17%, the share ai-timelines.md gives (0.15). Lo: war and coup risk, which arrive with AGI. Hi: slow-diffusion views, on which the excess builds over many years. It should grow with the lead (openQuestions).

referenceLeadYears.basis: Inferred from the five files. Their transition rates lean on forecasts and defences of 2026 to 2028 (FRI's biorisk conditionals for 2028, the FRI and GovAI grid pilot for 2026, Sentinel's forecasts for 2028, the Fed's 2026 AI-debt figures, Metaculus war questions to 2035) and on AGI in about 2027 to 2030 (ai-timelines.md: the weighted centre moved to 2027-2029 in November 2026; Metaculus strong AGI 2030). Centre 2028.5, plus about 3.5 years to full automation, is 2032: five years from the start of 2027. The 3.5 is above the three fast-view figures cited under turbulentYears, because full automation as the reader is asked for it needs robots at scale, and far below slow-diffusion views; with 3 the reference would be 4.5 and with 5 it would be 6.5. By hazard: cyber and bio 4 to 5, economy 5 to 6, war 5 to 7. The existential figure of 0.2 fits a lead of 8 to 12 years and is treated separately.

Three more years bring verified screening into force and little else. Lo: mandatory screening and model safeguards return risk near baseline, as FRI's experts expect (https://forecastingresearch.org/ai-enabled-biorisk). Hi: no gain.
Seven more years allow universal screening and part of a ten-year countermeasure programme, if funded; attack-side biotechnology advances too.
Countermeasure platforms, detection and clean-air measures have had time to deploy; state programmes and accidents remain. Hi: defences unfunded while open biological models spread.
Floor of about 0.7: state programmes, accidents in accelerated research and attack-favouring biology do not depend on preparation.

pandemicModerate.mechanism: The transition excess is small (2.2% to 2.8% a year) and comes from human-caused releases once AI clears the remaining capability thresholds and automated laboratories remove the wet-lab bottleneck, net of better detection of natural outbreaks. Preparation that takes time: verifiable screening of synthesis orders and benchtop synthesisers (sixteen years, by my recollection of the first guidance in 2010, to a policy that binds only federally funded buyers, with 250 to 340 days more to implement), vaccine platforms (326 days for the first COVID-19 vaccines against a goal of 100), and stockpiles, detection and clean air on the ten-year scale of the Apollo programme for biodefense. With little lead none of it is in place, but a release takes months of physical work and an epidemic months to spread, so the yearly rate rises less than for software hazards. With a long lead the excess falls slowly and not far: state programmes and laboratory accidents are untouched by screening, biotechnology itself advances, and more years pass in which capable open models exist (the model counts those years at today's rate). Floor assumed: 0.7 at 30 years.

evidence.claim: FRI (1 July 2025, revised 30 April 2026): the median expert put a human-caused epidemic of 100,000 deaths in 2028 at 0.3% a year, 1.5% conditional on several LLM capabilities, and 'close to baseline (0.4%)' when strict model safeguards and mandatory nucleic acid screening are adopted (from 1.25% in the scenario tested).

White House memorandum NSTM-6, 5 November 2026: the National Policy for Nucleic Acid Synthesis Screening 'requires all recipients of Federal life sciences funding to procure synthetic nucleic acids and benchtop synthesis equipment exclusively from certified suppliers'; NIST standards within 90 days, first list of adherent suppliers within 160 days, procurement from certified suppliers within 250 days and benchtop equipment within 340 days. It replaces the 2024 Framework and, on full implementation, the 2023 HHS guidance; 'Existing Federal guidance has relied on self-attestation'.

CEPI: the 100 Days Mission 'aims to develop safe, effective and accessible vaccines within 100 days of identifying a new pandemic threat'; for COVID-19, 'Within just 326 days, the first safe and effective vaccines were being rolled out.'

Bipartisan Commission on Biodefense, January 2021: the Apollo Program for Biodefense 'could effectively end the era of pandemic threats by 2030'; 'Even the most ambitious program (about $10 billion annually) would be a small fraction of the current cost'. A ten-year programme, proposed and not funded at that scale (the last clause is my recollection).

That the first federal screening guidance dates from 2010 is my recollection; the White House memorandum names only the 2023 HHS guidance and the 2024 Framework. International AI Safety Report 2026: 61.5% of the biological AI tools with high misuse potential are fully open source (from the sibling file, not re-read).

pandemicSevere.mechanism: As for pandemicModerate, but the excess is larger (0.4% to 1.5% a year) and comes mostly from deliberate releases selected for severity. FRI's experts put the yearly chance of a human-caused epidemic at 0.3%, at 1.5% once several AI capabilities exist, and back near baseline (0.4%) with strict model safeguards and legally mandatory synthesis screening. So the part of the excess due to lone actors is removable, and what it takes is regulation, which has moved slowly: guidance in 2010 (my recollection), a revision in 2023, a framework in 2024, and in November 2026 a policy for federally funded buyers only. Detection, rapid vaccines, protective equipment and clean air need about a decade of funded work. A short lead leaves 2026 defences facing full capability, tempered by the months a release takes. A long lead helps less than in cyber: one success suffices, states and accidents lie outside screening, and Esvelt and Amodei argue that biology favours attack (ai-bio.md). More lead also means more years of misuse-capable models before automation, which the model counts at today's rate. Floor assumed: 0.72 at 30 years.

evidence.claim: FRI: median expert 0.3% a year for a human-caused epidemic in 2028; 'rose to 1.5% conditional on several hypothetical LLM capabilities'; 2.3% with capabilities combined; experts 'reduced their risk forecast close to baseline (0.4%)' with LLM safeguards and mandatory nucleic acid screening. Published 1 July 2025, revised 30 April 2026.

White House, 5 November 2026: the new screening policy 'conditions Federal funding on compliance with verifiable standards'; customers that receive Federal funding must procure from certified suppliers within 250 days and benchtop equipment within 340 days. It does not bind suppliers or buyers without Federal funds.
Bipartisan Commission on Biodefense, 2021: a programme of about $10 billion a year 'could effectively end the era of pandemic threats by 2030', that is, in about ten years.

MacAskill and Taylor (Forethought, 22 January 2026) put the value lost to catastrophes other than takeover higher on longer timelines: 'The number gets higher in longer timelines because there's a longer time of perils'; chance of avoiding them 98.5%, 97% and 95.5% (MacAskill) if AI research is automated by 2027, 2035 and 2045. More lead means more cumulative exposure before automation, though less per year.

FRI LEAP wave 9 (30 June 2026), median expert: an AI-related catastrophe killing over 10% of people within five years has probability 0.08%, 1% and 2% by 2030, 2050 and 2100 under slow AI progress, and 1%, 5% and 10% under rapid progress.

Esvelt (October 2026): 'a reactive vaccine strategy is nearly useless against anyone capable of continually releasing new pandemics'; Amodei (January 2026): 'an asymmetry between attack and defense in biology'. Taken from the sibling file, not re-read.

cyberOutage.mechanism: The transition rate is driven by attacks on grid control systems by whoever holds an unsafeguarded AGI-level model, by state sabotage of data centres and their power supply during the race, and by accidents in AI-run operations. Preparation that takes time: control equipment is replaced on a 10-to-15-year cycle against 3 to 5 for office IT, so hardening comes through segmentation and monitoring in years and through replacement in decades; moving data centres onto their own generation takes years; restraint on attacking civilian infrastructure needs agreements of the kind that took decades for nuclear weapons. A short lead compresses the race, so that sabotage and access already held (at least five years for Volt Typhoon, per CISA in ai-cyber.md) are used against today's grid. A long lead lets utilities harden, but more AI load sits on shared grids, and state sabotage is a decision, not a vulnerability. Floor assumed: 0.6 at 30 years.

evidence.claim: NIST SP 800-82r3 (2023): 'Typical IT components have a lifetime on the order of three to five years'; for operational technology 'the lifetime of the deployed technology is often in the order of 10 to 15 years and sometimes longer.'

Anthropic, 2 June 2026: 'within 6 to 12 months, we expect that many other AI companies will have Mythos-class models'; 'the bottleneck in cybersecurity is now verifying, disclosing, and patching'; it hopes 'to enable a permanent advantage for defenders'.

Garfinkel and Dafoe (2019): for cyberattacks that exploit software vulnerabilities, 'growth in investments will favor offense when investment levels are sufficiently low' and 'favor defense when they are sufficiently high'.

Sentinel, 19 November 2026: 33% (10% to 60%) that by the end of 2028 an outage cuts power, telecoms, digital payments or water to over a million people in an OECD country for a week; the good case is one where 'companies notice vulnerabilities and fix their whole stack before it is too late'. No forecast is conditional on when AGI or automation arrives.

Hendrycks, Schmidt and Wang: states 'will act to disable threatening AI projects', up to 'Kinetic attacks on datacenters or corresponding power plants'; NERC, September 2026: data centres dropped up to 'nearly 4 GW' off the grid after routine faults; open models trail the frontier by '4 to 7 months' (AISI). Taken from the sibling file, not re-read.

gridLong.mechanism: A grid failure of weeks needs physical damage to long-lead equipment or an attacker able to defeat many restorations at once (GovAI, in ai-cyber.md); the transition figure adds escalation to kinetic attack on data centres and power plants. Preparation: spare large transformers (lead times now as long as four years), black-start and restoration drills, replacement of control equipment (10 to 15 years), and the arrangements between states that keep sabotage from escalating. None of this can be done in one to three years. Its factor lies between cyberOutage and greatPowerWar at every lead, because its two routes are theirs. With a long lead, spares and hardening accumulate, but the physical route is tied to war risk, which falls slowly. Floor assumed: 0.65 at 30 years.

waterSystemFailure.mechanism: Water is the softest utility: tens of thousands of small systems, old controllers reachable from the internet, no security staff (ai-cyber.md). A short lead raises the rate less than for power, because these attackers need time to take up new tools. A long lead helps slowly at first (small utilities adopt last, and equipment lasts 10 to 15 years or more) and more later, since the cheap fixes can be mandated and applied within a decade. Floor assumed: 0.57 at 30 years.

paymentsOutage.mechanism: Payments are software, concentrated in a few processors, and the transition figure assumes AGI-level offence in many hands against today's estates. Exploitation now begins on average seven days before a patch exists; the median organisation takes 43 days to patch, up from 32, and fully fixes 26% of known-exploited flaws; and in June 2026 Anthropic expected Mythos-class models at many companies within 6 to 12 months. Defence can catch up, and finance is the best-resourced and most regulated defender: flaws found by AI can be fixed before attackers find them, new code can be written memory-safe (Android cut the memory-safety share of its vulnerabilities from 76% in 2019 to an expected 24% in 2024), and resilience rules take a few years to adopt and apply (the EU's DORA: regulation of December 2022, binding from January 2025). Against that, core banking systems last decades and the patching burden is rising. This is still the hazard where lead time helps most: I take the excess to fall by a quarter with three more years and by half with seven. A short lead does the reverse. Floor assumed: 0.33 at 30 years, for state attack on finance, concentration, and failures caused by AI-run operations and rushed patching.

bankingCrisis.mechanism: The transition figure rests on a jump in real interest rates, runs made faster by AI agents, erosion of the tax base and the bust of a debt-financed AI boom. Speed matters in the record: after three years of rapid growth in credit and asset prices the chance of a crisis within three years is about 40%, against 7% in normal times. A faster transition means a faster boom, a sharper repricing and no time for supervisors, whose rule-making runs on a ten-year clock (Basel III: published 2010, final reforms endorsed 2017, transitional arrangements to 2028). A slower one lets balance sheets, rate expectations and rules adjust. Two things limit the gain: rates must reprice however long the wait, and with a long lead the AI boom of 2026 may bust first because AI came slower than priced, a risk that falls in the next few years and that this factor does not capture. A crisis also takes a year or more to brew, which tempers the factor at one year and moves part of it after automation. Floor assumed: 0.63 at 30 years.

evidence.claim: Greenwood, Hanson, Shleifer and Sorensen (NBER 27396; Journal of Finance 2022): rapid credit and asset-price growth over three years is followed by 'about a 40% probability of entering a financial crisis within the next three years'; 'This compares with a roughly 7% probability in normal times'.

Basel Committee: the first phase of Basel III was 'originally published in December 2010'; the post-crisis reforms were endorsed on '7 December 2017'; the summary of phase-in is titled 'Basel III transitional arrangements, 2017-2028'.

Korinek and Suh (NBER 32255, 2024): 'The effects on wages depend on a race between automation and capital accumulation'; 'if the complexity of tasks that humans can perform is bounded and full automation is reached, then wages collapse.' The speed of automation, not its extent, sets the shock to household income and so to loan books.

Federal Reserve, November 2026: large banks have 'close to $1 trillion of exposure' to AI-related borrowers; AI debt issuance 'more than $680 billion by October 2026' against '$130 billion in all of 2023'. Taken from the sibling file, not re-read.

supplyShock.mechanism: The excess over today (5% to 8% a year in the US) is strikes and protest over automation, trade disruption from conflict between the AI powers, and panic buying in financial or cyber crises. Labour markets adjust slowly: places hit by Chinese import competition, which plateaued in 2010, were still depressed in 2019, and in 1830 threshing machines caused riots, fewer where other work was available. If automation is slow enough, wages can keep rising. So a longer lead means fewer workers displaced per year, more time for transfers and retraining, and less disruption. A short lead means more, limited at one year by the time strikes and shortages take to organise. Floor assumed: 0.63 at 30 years, since full automation ends most paid work however long it takes.

Narayanan and Kapoor (2025): 'Diffusion occurs over decades, not years'; adaptation is limited by how quickly 'not only individuals, but also organizations and institutions, can adapt to technology.'

aiFraud.mechanism: The excess is real-time voice and video cloning and automated targeting against authentication built for an earlier threat. Lead time matters least here. Fraud depends on criminals taking up tools, which lags capability, so a short lead raises the rate only a little. Defences take five to eight years and displace fraud more than they end it: US chip cards went from under 5% of in-person transactions in 2015 to nearly 90% in 2022, and counterfeit fraud fell on one kind of network and returned to its 2015 level on the other. A longer lead also gives criminals more years with capable models, so the excess barely falls. FRI's experts expect cybercrime losses only 1.5 times higher in 2031 under rapid than under slow AI progress. Floor assumed: 0.8 at 30 years.

greatPowerWar.mechanism: The transition figure triples the US-China rate for preventive attack, sabotage that escalates, and Taiwan's place in chip supply. Theory makes speed the cause: Powell shows that large, rapid shifts in the distribution of power can lead to war, because the rising side cannot commit to restraint; a slower shift leaves room for bargains. Time also allows agreements, though slowly: SALT I took two and a half years of talks and came 27 years after the first bomb, and the non-proliferation treaty took seven years from proposal to signature. Against this, a longer lead means a longer arms race, and MacAskill and Taylor put China's chance of a decisive advantage at 10%, 30% and 50% on short, medium and long timelines: a contest between near-equals in place of a US lead, though RAND finds preventive attack relatively more likely where one side has a monopoly to preserve. I take the excess to fall slowly and not far, to 0.77 at 30 years, with a range from 0.22 to 1.7: the sign is not settled. At a one-year lead the shift is largest, but wars take time to decide and mobilise, and one side may prevail before the other can act.

evidence.claim: Powell, 'War as a Commitment Problem' (International Organization, 2006): in preventive war, pre-emptive attack and conflicts over future bargaining power alike, 'large, rapid shifts in the distribution of power can lead to war.'

nuclearNear.mechanism: The transition figure multiplies great-power nuclear risk by 2 to 2.5 for threats to second-strike forces, shorter decision times, AI in warning systems and escalation from conventional war. All four are worse the faster the shift: Cotton-Barratt names the rapidity of change as raising the risk, because things may move too fast for a peaceful division of power to be found. Given years, states adapt their forces (more warheads, mobile launchers, launch on warning) and deterrence holds, though those adaptations raise the risk of accident and a longer race means larger arsenals. Agreements take decades. Floor assumed: 0.78 at 30 years, with an upper bound well above 1.

civilUnrest.mechanism: The US transition figure adds to the base rate 0.5 points for a seizure of power and 0.8 for unrest over jobs and opposition to AI. For the first there is a forecast by lead time: MacAskill and Taylor put the risk of a coup in the US, given that the US dominates, at 22%, 10% and 7% if AI research is automated by 2027, 2035 and 2045, ratios of 0.45 and 0.32. The chance that the US dominates falls too (85%, 55%, 35%), so the unconditional fall may be steeper; I use the conditional ratios and shade the result up, because the factor also serves places where a seizure of power is a small part of the excess. For the second part, the speed of displacement is what matters: machines caused the Swing riots, less where other work softened the blow; the China shock was still visible nine years after it levelled off; and rules and transfers take years to pass and apply (the EU's AI Act: in force 2024, high-risk rules 2027 to 2028). At a one-year lead unrest lags the shock, so part of it falls after automation. Floor assumed: 0.55 at 30 years.

evidence.claim: MacAskill and Taylor (Forethought, 22 January 2026): 'Coup risk in the US (conditional on US dominance) is something like 22%/10%/7% on short/medium/long timelines', defined as AI research fully automated by the end of 2027, 2035 and 2045. The US 'becomes less likely to get a DSA on longer timelines (say, 85%/55%/35%)', so the figures are conditional on something whose chance also falls. The chance of avoiding extreme power concentration is 80.1%, 86.5% and 80.1% (MacAskill), not monotonic, because China's share of power rises with time.

afterShare.mechanism: Full automation is a capability milestone, not the end of the turbulence. The old research put the transition at the five years from AGI; with automation about 3.5 years after AGI at the reference, and sooner at shorter leads, part of that window lies after automation. The engine carries it as a share of the way from the after rate back to the transition rate, fading to zero over the 3.5 turbulent years, so a share s adds 1.75 x s year-equivalents of turbulence. I set s so that this matches the part of the old window that falls after automation, less a discount for front-loading. No source says how fast hazards fall after automation. On the check's criterion, that five-year risk should not fall the sooner automation comes: with these figures the software and power hazards are about level for automation from 2028 to 2031 (cyberOutage 1.02%, 1.09%, 1.03%, 0.98% a year; across the six of them 2028 is at most 15% below the peak), and the criterion fails for 2027 and for the slow-fuse hazards, for reasons given in openQuestions. The check proposed 0.7 at one year and 0.3 at three for a share that did not fade and a turbulent period of five years; the figures here give about the same five-year totals under the engine as it now is.

existential.mechanism: The chance of existential catastrophe given AGI is the one figure for which forecasts by arrival date exist, and almost all point the same way. In a 2022 thread about 40 forecasters gave it for five arrival windows; without two people counted twice, the medians fall from 70% (2025 to 2030) to 63% (2030 to 2040), 45% (2040 to 2060) and 34% (after 2060), and of the 37 who answered every window two rise after the second. Metaculus, on a narrower question (a fall of more than 95% in world population from AI within 25 years of AGI), shows 40% for arrival in 2025 to 2029, 30% for 2030 to 2039, 17% for 2040 to 2059 and 11% for 2060 to 2099. Greenblatt's estimates of takeover fall from 45% with no lead for safety work to 20% with months, 13% with one to three years and 7% with ten; his lead is time bought at the critical moment, not years until AGI, so using it for a short lead is an analogy. The mechanisms: more years of alignment and control research, with more capable assistants and more warning, and a slower takeoff (MacAskill and Taylor; Davidson); against them, a compute overhang that could make a late takeoff very fast (Kokotajlo), and less influence for those now working on the problem. The engine now applies the factor to the odds, so I read the sources as ratios of odds: at five years 1.16 to 1.32, where the ratios of probabilities are 1.05 to 1.16, because the sources start from levels between 35% and 67%. The sources agree about as well on either scale at short leads and better on the odds at long ones (0.37 to 0.47 against 0.48 to 0.67 at about 26 years); whether an odds ratio carries down to the model's 0.2 is an assumption. Mapping: a window stands for a lead equal to its midpoint (of the part still ahead) plus 3.5 years, less 2027: about 5, 11.5 and 26.5. The existing figure of 0.2 comes from statements of 2020 to 2024 by people whose median AGI dates were then in the 2030s and 2040s, so the factor is 1 at eight years, not five. All seven factors are guesses: the mapping, the reference and the weighting of the sources are mine. Floor assumed: 0.42 at 30 years, where the sources stand.

evidence.claim: Lifland's forecasting thread (LessWrong, 14 September 2022) asked for the chance of an AI-caused existential catastrophe conditional on AGI arriving by 2025, in 2025-2030, 2030-2040, 2040-2060 and after 2060. Lifland's own answers: 65%, 60%, 55%, 50%, 45%. Greenblatt: 73, 53, 41, 30, 28. Finnveden: 80, 50, 35, 25, 20. Grace: 14, 12, 11, 8, 4. Medians of the 41 to 45 answers per window, my computation: 84.5, 74, 65, 46, 34.5. Two people are counted twice (Kokotajlo under two names and, per the check, Sharmake, who appears in my copy also as Noosphere89); without the second entries the medians are 83, 70, 63, 45, 34. Of the 37 people who answered all five windows, two rise after the second (sbowman 25, 18, 15, 35, 45; weeatquince 15, 12, 8, 4, 5). The fetch tool rebuilt the lists from the page's layout; the check confirmed the medians against LessWrong's poll data.

Metaculus question 12840, 'How does the level of existential risk posed by AGI depend on its arrival time?', resolves yes for a window if AGI (question 5121) arrives in it 'AND the global population declines by more than 95% due to an artificial intelligence failure mode within a period of 25 years starting from the time at which AGI was developed'. Community figures read from the data in the embed page on 20 November 2026: arrival 2025 to 2029, 40% (79 forecasters; mean 42%); 2030 to 2039, 30% (100; mean 35%); 2040 to 2059, 17% (99; mean 27%); 2060 to 2099, 11% (99; mean 20%); 2022 to 2024, 20%, a window that has passed. 111 forecasters in all. A narrower event than Lifland's.
Dickens (12 July 2025) on the same Metaculus question: 'Answers range from 50% to 9.3% depending on date range'. Those were the figures of July 2025; the highest is now 40%.

Greenblatt (8 October 2025), takeover risk by 'how much lead time we have to spend on x-risk focused safety work': 'Plan A: 10 years' 7%; 'Plan B: 1-3 years' 13%; 'Plan C: 1-9 months (probably on the lower end of this)' 20%; 'Plan D: ~0 months, but ten people on the inside doing helpful things' 45%; Plan E 75%. Probabilities of each world: 5%, 10%, 25%, 45%, 15%, which average to 38%; plans D and E alone average 52%, a ratio of 1.38 in probability and 1.8 in odds; plans C, D and E average 43%. The lead is time bought for safety at the critical moment, by agreement or a lead over rivals, not years until AGI.

MacAskill and Taylor (22 January 2026): 'The default probability of averting AI takeover is higher on medium and longer timelines'; 'On longer timelines, takeoff is likely slower'; 'we expect AI takeover risk is higher if takeoff is faster'; 'it seems quite likely that the overall level of risk is lower on longer timelines'. They give no takeover probability by timeline.

FRI LEAP wave 9 (survey of May to June 2026), median expert: AI-related catastrophe (over 10% of people dead within five years) by 2100 at 2% if AI by 2030 'is merely a capable assistant to human workers' and 10% if it 'can match or surpass the best humans across cognitive and physical tasks'.
Davidson (23 January 2023): 'The easier AGI is to develop, the faster takeoff will be.' With lower training requirements, about 40% for a takeoff under one year against 25%.

AI Futures Project (31 December 2025): 'Faster takeoffs are also correlated in our model with shorter timelines'; Kokotajlo doubts it: 'on longer timelines, takeoff should be extremely fast due to the vast amounts of compute that will have piled up by then.' Lifland: automated coder to ASI in under one year 30%, under three years 60%.

openQuestions: The run-up and the turbulent period should grow with the lead; the engine keeps both fixed. Rule I would use: turbulent years T(L) = the smaller of L and 3.5 + 0.1 x (L - 5) beyond five years (3.8, 4.2, 5 and 6 at 8, 12, 20 and 30); run-up R(L) = L - T(L), so that the excess is zero at the start of 2027, where today's rate is observed, and reaches its full level when the turbulent period begins, rising with the square of the time elapsed (most of the rise comes late). If T grows like this, multiply the factors beyond five years by 3.5 / T(L) (0.92, 0.83, 0.7, 0.58) so that the whole excess is unchanged.

With the run-up fixed at two years, a reader who gives 2037 or later gets no AI effect in the next five years, and one who gives 2036 very little. Under the rule above a 2040 reader would average about a tenth of the full excess over the next five years. Two near-term risks are also left out at long leads: Sentinel's forecasts (33% for a week-long OECD outage by the end of 2028) assume no AGI, so cyber risk may keep rising through the late 2020s whatever the year; and a reader whose year is later than markets expect faces the bust of the 2026 AI debt boom.

A step remains at 2027 for years before 2032, because the ramp is anchored to the year of automation: for 2031 the rate starts 2027 at half the full excess, for 2030 or earlier at all of it, against an observed rate with no excess. The rule above removes it for every year whose turbulent period starts after 2027; for earlier years a ramp of a year or so from today's rate would.

For a reader who gives 2027 the five-year risk is lower than for 2028 (cyberOutage 0.6% a year against 1.0%), against the premise. Only half a year lies before automation; the factor is held flat below a lead of one year, so only half of the one-year excess is counted; and the tail holds at most 1.75 year-equivalents. Letting the factor rise as 1 / L below one year (the same turbulence in less time) would give about 0.87%.

One afterShare serves all hazards. For the slow-fuse hazards (fraud, unrest, banking crises, pandemics) more of a rushed transition falls after automation than the cap allows, so their five-year risk is lower for 2028 than for 2030 (aiFraud 9.7% against 11.3% a year in the US). A share per hazard would fix it. Where the after rate is far below today's (moderate pandemics, war), five-year risk also falls for the earliest years because the safer world of the old research arrives sooner; that comes from the after rates, not from these factors.

Existential risk with a short lead. The engine spreads the chance from 2027 to automation, so for 2027 or 2028 all of it falls in the first six to eighteen months. AI 2027 puts takeover about a year after people become obsolete. I would spread it over at least three years, running past automation when fewer than three turbulent years remain.
The reference differs by hazard: about 4 to 5 years for cyber and bio, 5 to 6 for the economy, 5 to 7 for war, 8 to 12 for the existential figure. Only the last is reflected in the table.

The factors do not vary by place. Buenos Aires meets war and nuclear risk only indirectly, and its utilities and banks are the trailing-edge defenders for whom lead time helps latest. The civilUnrest factor is weighted for the US, where a seizure of power is 38% of the excess, and rests on coup figures conditional on US dominance.

Whether longer timelines mean a slower takeoff is disputed: Davidson and MacAskill and Taylor say yes, Kokotajlo that a compute overhang could make a late takeoff very fast. The high ends at 20 and 30 years (1.2 or more for every hazard) allow for it; the middles do not.

Because all AI figures share one draw, the low end of each factor is paired with the sceptic's rates and the high end with the highly concerned view. I oriented the ranges for that (beyond five years, low means that defenders adapt quickly given time), but the pairing was not part of the brief.

No forecaster has been asked the question the model needs. A small panel (Sentinel, Samotsvety, FRI) could answer it directly: the yearly chance of a week-long outage, a banking crisis or a great-power war in the years before and after full automation, given automation in 2030, 2035 and 2045.
